items.followUp: What is photophosphorylation, and how do cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation differ?

rubric.why: Identifies the electron pathway represented by the Z-scheme.
rubric.description: States that electrons move non-cyclically from water through photosystems II and I to NADP.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the non-cyclic electron pathway and its route.

rubric.why: Explains why the pathway is called the Z-scheme.
rubric.description: States that the energy changes of the electrons form a pattern resembling the letter Z.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the Z-shaped energy pattern.

modelAnswer: The Z-scheme is the noncyclic movement of electrons from water through photosystem II and photosystem I to NADP.
The energy-level changes of the electrons during this pathway form a pattern resembling the letter Z.

items.followUp: Explain how evaporation from leaves causes water to rise in xylem vessels.

rubric.why: Defines transpiration pull as an upward force acting on water in the xylem.
rubric.description: Defines transpiration pull as the force that draws water upward through the xylem.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving the upward pull of water through xylem as the definition.

rubric.why: Explains how water loss from leaves creates the pull on the water column.
rubric.description: Explains that evaporation from leaves creates tension that pulls the continuous water column upward from the roots.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking evaporation from leaves to tension and the upward movement of water.

modelAnswer: Transpiration pull is the force that draws water upward through the xylem of a plant.
Evaporation of water from leaf surfaces creates tension, which pulls the continuous column of water up from the roots.

items.followUp: Trace the path of blood in systemic circulation, naming the chambers and major blood vessels involved.

rubric.why: Identifies the route carrying blood from the heart to the lungs.
rubric.description: States that blood travels from the right ventricle through the pulmonary artery to the lungs.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct heart-to-lungs route.

rubric.why: Identifies the route by which blood returns from the lungs to the heart.
rubric.description: States that blood returns from the lungs through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct lungs-to-heart return route.

modelAnswer: Pulmonary circulation is the circulation of blood from the right ventricle of the heart to the lungs and back to the heart.
Blood travels to the lungs through the pulmonary artery and returns to the left atrium through the pulmonary veins.

items.followUp: Explain the lock-and-key model of enzyme action and state what happens to the enzyme after the reaction.

rubric.why: Identifies where the substrate attaches to the enzyme.
rubric.description: States that the substrate binds to the enzyme's active site.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the active site as the substrate-binding region.

rubric.why: Explains the specific fit between an enzyme and its substrate.
rubric.description: States that the active site's shape is complementary to the substrate, like a key fitting a lock.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining the complementary fit.

rubric.why: Names the temporary intermediate in enzyme action.
rubric.description: States that a temporary enzyme-substrate complex forms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the enzyme-substrate complex.

rubric.why: Describes the products being released and the enzyme remaining available for reuse.
rubric.description: States that products are released and the enzyme remains unchanged and can be used again.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the enzyme is unchanged and reusable after the reaction.

modelAnswer: The substrate binds to the enzyme's active site, whose shape is complementary to the substrate, like a key fitting a lock.
The enzyme converts the substrate into product or products, which are then released.
The enzyme remains unchanged and can be used again.
